newsitem.title: FRANCE: Delors says EU reform conference on wrong track.
newsitem.headline: Delors says EU reform conference on wrong track.

text.p: The European Union is in danger of failing in the main aim of its reform conference because member states are trying to do too much, former European Commission President Jacques Delors said on Thursday.

Delors, who as Commission chief from 1985-95 was one of the architects of the Maastricht treaty, said the 15-nation bloc should concentrate on reforming its institutions to make way for enlargement to central and eastern Europe.
"I fear the agenda of the inter-governmental conference (IGC) is too overloaded and we will miss the essential aim," he told a news conference. "They are trying to tackle too many issues."
"We have to get straight down to essentials and do things simply," he said.
"What is essential today is to tell our eastern brothers that we are preparing a treaty that will enable them to join us when the conditions are met," Delors said.

He said the EU's central problem was that institutions created for a six-nation community in 1957 were creaking at the seams with the current 15 members and could not possibly work with up to 30 in the next decade.
Asked what issues should be given less importance in the IGC, he said attempts to build a common foreign and security policy and increase cooperation on police and justice affairs.

Since it opened in Italy last March, the IGC has spent much time on such inter-governmental matters, partly because the central questions of reforming the majority voting system and the size and powers of the European Commission and the European Parliament are so difficult, diplomats say.
"It's not enough to design a good-looking car. You have to lift the bonnet and see how the engine works," Delors said.
There would soon be so many member states that in normal Council of Ministers discussions, it would take three to four hours to go around the table with delegations stating their position, he said.
He quoted French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette as saying the new EU Council chamber was so big that he could not even see who was sitting at the other side of the table.
